flashcards.q: Define leakage in one sentence, and give an example beyond 'label as a feature'.
flashcards.a: Information available at training time that would not be available at prediction time. Example: 'days since account marked for closure' predicting churn -- the feature only exists because churn already happened.

flashcards.q: Why is random k-fold CV invalid for time-series data?
flashcards.a: K-fold validity assumes exchangeability (rows are interchangeable). Time-series rows have autocorrelation/trend, and production only ever sees strictly-past data when predicting -- random k-fold can put future rows in training and past rows in validation, an impossible scenario in production.

flashcards.q: Why must target encoding be computed with CV-fold isolation?
flashcards.a: Naive target encoding uses the full training set including the row being encoded, so that row's own label contributes to its own feature value. Fix: encode each fold using only the OTHER folds' statistics.

flashcards.q: Why does GroupKFold matter for data with multiple rows per entity (user/patient/store)?
flashcards.a: Random k-fold can split one entity's rows across train and validation, letting the model memorize entity-specific idiosyncrasies rather than generalizing -- inflating validation metrics relative to true performance on a genuinely new, unseen entity, which is what production needs.

flashcards.q: Train/test contamination vs temporal leakage -- what's the distinction?
flashcards.a: Train/test contamination: a procedural error, fitting preprocessing (scaler/imputer/encoder) on data including validation/test rows. Temporal leakage: a feature-construction error, a feature's value reflects information from after its own prediction timestamp. Both can coexist in the same pipeline; fixing one doesn't fix the other.

flashcards.q: What optimistic bias does nested CV remove that single-loop CV has?
flashcards.a: Using the same CV loop for both hyperparameter selection and final reporting means the chosen hyperparameter was picked because it performed best on those specific validation folds -- an information leak into the reported number. Nested CV uses an inner loop for tuning within each outer training fold, keeping the outer validation fold untouched until the final honest evaluation.

Pandas' rolling window is inclusive of the current row by default -- if the feature should mean 'prior N days, not including today,' it leaks the current row's own value into its own feature. Fix: shift by 1 (or by the real reporting lag) before rolling.

flashcards.q: Why does an implausibly high validation metric function as a leakage red flag on its own?
flashcards.a: Genuine performance improvements on well-studied problems tend to come in modest increments; a sudden large jump is statistically more likely to be an information shortcut (leakage) than a breakthrough, since leakage bugs are common and breakthroughs of that magnitude are rare.

flashcards.q: Expanding window vs rolling window in time-series CV -- when to use which?
flashcards.a: Expanding window (train grows: Jan-Mar->val Apr, Jan-Apr->val May) uses all available past data, best when the process is stable. Rolling (fixed trailing size) window is better when older data is stale or a genuine distribution shift/regime change has occurred.
